svg.aria-label: Diagram: how AWS Payment Cryptography separates a key's identity from its key material, and what each lifecycle operation therefore acts on. Payment Cryptography keys are used for all cryptographic functions and are either generated using the create key command or added by calling key import, with the origin recorded in the KeyOrigin attribute. Keys have key types principally defined by ANSI X9 TR 31 that restrict their use to their intended purpose as specified in PCI PIN v3.1 Requirement 19, and attributes are bound to keys using key blocks when stored, shared with other accounts, or exported, as specified in PCI PIN v3.1 Requirement 18-3. The central structural fact is that a key is identified by an ARN which, in AWS's words, is not related or derived from the key material, and because ARNs are automatically assigned during create or import operations these values are not idempotent. AWS states the consequence twice on one page: importing the same key multiple times will result in multiple key ARNs with their own lifecycle, and the same key material will be located under multiple key ARNs but each with a different key lifecycle. The service deliberately does not deduplicate on material, and two opposite consequences follow. The first is a false sense of completion, because scheduling deletion of the ARN an application references and letting the waiting period expire removes that key while the same material may remain live under another ARN imported during an earlier migration, so the key inventory shrinks while cryptographic exposure does not. The second is a false alarm, because two ARNs holding identical material are indistinguishable from two distinct keys in any listing, so an audit counting keys over-counts secrets and a rotation replacing one ARN leaves the other serving. The nearest available signal is the key check value, since the API returns KeyCheckValue and KeyCheckValueAlgorithm on every key, but AWS defines a KCV as a variety of checksum methods used to compare keys to each other without having access to the actual key material, computed by retaining only the 3 highest order bytes of the result, which is 24 bits. A matching KCV therefore identifies keys that may contain the same material and does not conclusively prove the material is identical, so matching values flag potential duplicates for further verification, recorded with the algorithm because the computation differs between TDES and AES keys and with KeyOrigin because an imported duplicate is the case that matters. On attributes, keys have both immutable and mutable attributes defined at creation: algorithm, length and usage are defined at creation and cannot be changed, while effective date and expiration date can be modified. Certain keys can only be created with certain key modes of use, aligned whenever possible with TR-31, and the service prevents creation of invalid keys, which is the correct enforcement point because a documentation table can go stale and an API check cannot. The operational consequence is that there is no such thing as adjusting a key: a key whose modes of use are wrong must be replaced, producing a new ARN, which is why aliases exist. An alias is a user-friendly name associated with a key, up to 256 characters, always beginning with alias slash, that allows keys to be rotated or otherwise changed without impacting application code, so application code should reference aliases from the outset. On deletion, Payment Cryptography never deletes keys belonging to active AWS accounts unless deletion is explicitly scheduled and the mandatory waiting period expires. Because deleting a key is irreversible the service requires a waiting period of between 3 and 180 days, with a default of seven days, and the actual waiting period might be up to 24 hours longer than the one scheduled, so the real date should be read from the GetKey operations rather than computed. The point that matters operationally is that the waiting period is not a grace period for the workload: a key pending deletion cannot be used in any cryptographic operations, so scheduling deletion stops PIN verification against that key immediately. Two clocks run at once, and only one is a grace period: the recovery clock runs 3 to 180 days and is genuinely generous, while the availability clock runs out the instant DeleteKey is called. That is defensible, since a key declared for destruction should not keep authorising transactions, but it is the opposite of how the phrase waiting period reads and is the most expensive thing here to misunderstand. Deletion can be cancelled before the window ends but not after, and when it ends the service deletes the key, its aliases, and all related metadata. CloudTrail records an entry both when deletion is scheduled and when the key is actually deleted, which matters because the two moments are days apart and mean different things, one being the outage and the other the point of no return. On multi-Region replication, deleting a Primary Region key means the Replica Region keys are also automatically deleted, and a Replica Region key cannot be deleted like a Primary Region key; removing one requires modifying the replication regions of the primary. So a replica is not an independent object with its own lifecycle, unlike the duplicate-import case where two ARNs are independent, giving two superficially similar situations, the same material in two places, opposite lifecycle semantics depending on how it got there. Finally, closing or deleting the AWS account makes keys inaccessible rather than deleted, and deletion need not be scheduled separately from closing the account, which is the answer to a compliance question about key destruction and not the same answer the deletion path gives. The recommended audit is to list every key with its KeyCheckValue, KeyCheckValueAlgorithm and KeyOrigin and group by check value within each algorithm, since any group with more than one member is a potential duplicate-material group requiring further verification rather than a proven one, and then to check whether any system references a key ARN rather than an alias.
svg.title: Identity is independent of the secret, so the lifecycle acts on a handle
svg.text: Five words decide how this whole service behaves.
AWS Payment Cryptography — the ARN is “not related or derived from the key material”.
THE ARN — what has a lifecycle
“not related or derived from the key material”
“these values are not idempotent”
Enable, disable, schedule deletion, cancel, expire —
every one of them acts on this, not on the secret.
THE MATERIAL — what you care about
Governed by ANSI X9 TR 31 key types, “as specified
in PCI PIN v3.1 Requirement 19”.
Bound to attributes by key blocks when stored,
shared or exported.
So the same secret imported twice is two keys. AWS says it twice, which usually means somebody got caught.
“Importing the same key multiple times will result in multiple key ARNs with their own lifecycle.”
“the same key material will be located under multiple key ARNS but each with a different key lifecycle”
Delete the ARN your app uses and the material can still be live under another. The inventory shrinks; the exposure does not.
A matching KeyCheckValue screens for it — 24 bits of checksum, not proof. Verify before acting.
Two clocks start when you call DeleteKey, and only one of them is a grace period
RECOVERY 3 – 180 days (default 7, “up to 24 hours longer”) → generous, cancellable
AVAILABILITY runs out immediately → “cannot be used in any
cryptographic operations”
Scheduling is the outage. The date is only the point of no return — which is why CloudTrail logs both moments.
Read the real date from GetKey rather than computing it from your own schedule.
Fixed at creation, so corrections mean a new ARN
“algorithm, length, and usage are defined at creation
and cannot be changed”. Dates can move.
Which is why aliases exist: “rotated or otherwise changed
without impacting your application code”. Use them.
A replica is not a duplicate
Delete a Primary Region key and the Replica Region
keys “will also be automatically deleted”.
Same material in two places, opposite lifecycle rules —
it depends entirely on how it got there.
The audit
List KeyCheckValue, KeyCheckValueAlgorithm and KeyOrigin; group by value within an algorithm. A group above one is a candidate.
When you delete the thing, what exactly did you delete? Here the answer is: a handle. The secret may not have been in it alone.
